subject: chemistry
title: Optical isomerism
key_idea: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is a chiral centre. It gives two optical isomers, enantiomers, which are non-superimposable mirror images. They rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions, and an equal mixture, a racemic mixture, has no effect.

blocks.text: Optical isomerism is a type of stereoisomerism: the atoms are bonded in the same order but arranged differently in space. This section covers what causes it.

items.meaning: An asymmetric carbon atom, bonded to four different atoms or groups.
Optical isomers: a pair of molecules that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.
A molecule that cannot be superimposed on its mirror image.

items: A chiral centre has four different groups arranged tetrahedrally around the carbon.
There are two different ways to arrange four different groups in 3-D.
The two arrangements are mirror images, like left and right hands, and cannot be placed on top of each other.
A molecule with one chiral centre has exactly two enantiomers.
Draw the chiral carbon with two bonds in the plane of the paper.
Show one bond as a solid wedge (towards the viewer) and one as a dashed wedge (away from the viewer).
Draw the second enantiomer as the mirror image: reflect the first in a vertical line, keeping the same groups.
Swapping any two groups on the chiral centre gives the other enantiomer.
A chiral centre is a carbon bonded to four different groups.
Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images.
One chiral centre gives two enantiomers.

blocks.text: To find a chiral centre, look at each carbon atom in turn and ask whether its four groups are all different. This section gives a method and examples.

items.text: Ignore carbon atoms in C=C or C=O bonds, or with fewer than four attached groups. Ignore any carbon with two identical groups, such as CH₃ or CH₂.
For each remaining carbon, write down the four groups attached.
If all four groups are different, it is a chiral centre. Compare whole groups, not just the first atom.

items: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃: carbon 2 has H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃, so it is chiral.
2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid), CH₃CH(OH)COOH: carbon 2 has H, OH, CH₃ and COOH, so it is chiral.
Alanine, CH₃CH(NH₂)COOH, is chiral. Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, is not, because it has two H atoms on the central carbon.
Propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH, is not chiral, because carbon 2 has two CH₃ groups.

diagram.alt: Sort each molecule by whether it has a chiral centre.
diagram.prompt: Does the molecule contain a chiral centre?

items: Check every carbon: it is chiral only if all four attached groups differ.
A carbon with two identical groups (e.g. two H or two CH₃) cannot be chiral.
Compare whole groups, not single atoms.

blocks.text: Enantiomers have the same melting point, boiling point and chemical reactions, apart from reactions with other chiral molecules. They differ in how they affect plane-polarised light.

items.meaning: Light whose waves vibrate in one plane only. It is also monochromatic (one wavelength) when used to test optical activity.
The ability of a single enantiomer to rotate the plane of plane-polarised light.
A mixture of equal amounts of two enantiomers.

items: One enantiomer rotates the plane of polarisation clockwise; the other rotates it by the same angle anticlockwise.
A racemic mixture has equal and opposite rotations that cancel, so it is **optically inactive**.
Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties, except for this rotation and their reactions with other chiral molecules (such as enzymes).
In the nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde or an unsymmetrical ketone, the C=O group is trigonal planar.
The cyanide ion attacks from either side of the plane with equal probability.
Equal amounts of each enantiomer form, so the product is a racemic mixture, which is optically inactive.
Any reaction that forms a chiral centre from a flat starting group, with no chiral influence, gives a racemic mixture.
Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarised light, by equal angles in opposite directions.
A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mixture of enantiomers and is optically inactive.
Racemates form when a planar group is attacked equally from both sides.

checks.q: Explain what is meant by a chiral centre, and identify it in 2-chlorobutane, CH₃CHClCH₂CH₃.
checks.a: A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different atoms or groups. In 2-chlorobutane it is carbon 2, which is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃.

checks.q: State two ways in which the two enantiomers of a compound are the same and one way in which they differ.
checks.a: They have the same melting point and boiling point (or the same chemical reactions). They differ in the direction in which they rotate the plane of plane-polarised light.

checks.q: HCN adds to ethanal, CH₃CHO, to form 2-hydroxypropanenitrile. Explain why the product does not rotate plane-polarised light.
checks.a: The C=O group is planar, so cyanide ions attack from either side with equal probability. Equal amounts of the two enantiomers form, which is a racemic mixture. Their rotations cancel, so the mixture is optically inactive.

blocks.text: This part covers how optical activity gives evidence about the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution of a haloalkane.

items: Start with a single enantiomer of a chiral haloalkane, which is optically active, and measure the product.
**SN₁**: the haloalkane first forms a planar carbocation. The nucleophile attacks from either side equally, so a racemic mixture forms. The product is optically inactive.
**SN₂**: the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite to the leaving group in one step. The product is a single enantiomer, with the arrangement inverted, and it stays optically active.
So an optically active reactant that gives an optically inactive product points to SN₁. One that gives an optically active product points to SN₂.

blocks.text: This part covers why chirality matters when drug molecules are made. A compound can contain more than one chiral centre, but meso compounds are not needed.

items: The two enantiomers of a drug can have **different biological activity**. One may be the useful drug while the other is inactive or harmful.
Many chemical syntheses make a racemic mixture, so the two enantiomers must be separated to obtain a pure drug.
Separation is difficult and costly, because enantiomers have the same physical properties.
A **chiral catalyst** can be used to make one enantiomer only, so no separation is needed and waste is reduced.
Use the terms: optically active means the sample rotates plane-polarised light; a racemic mixture is equal amounts of two enantiomers and is not optically active.
